lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The library was not a place of learning. It was a graveyard of drafts.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek stumbled through the doorway as it sealed behind them, the calcified key fused to his left hand scraping against the obsidian floor. Gray necrosis had climbed past his elbow now, spreading in delicate branching lines beneath his skin. Every heartbeat forced something thick and cold through the veins that remained. It no longer felt like blood. The sensation had settled into something stranger, as though ink itself had replaced whatever the City had already taken.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Ahead of him, Ninsun slowed just enough to study the room before continuing. She no longer glanced toward corners or searched for hidden exits. Somewhere during their descent she had abandoned the hope that every chamber concealed another way out. Now she looked only for patterns—for repetitions in the stonework, for symbols carved where they did not belong, for the quiet logic that held the City together beneath all its contradictions.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The chamber stretched beyond the reach of the torchlight. Black shelves rose in impossible rows, climbing into darkness so complete that they appeared to dissolve before reaching a ceiling. Upon them rested thousands of glass jars, each identical in size despite containing scenes that could not possibly fit inside. Some glowed with a pale, rhythmic light while others remained dark, yet even those seemed to pulse faintly whenever the City's distant breathing rolled through the floor beneath their feet.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: There was no smell of parchment or old leather, none of the familiar scents a library should have carried. The air tasted instead of dry stone, cold glass, and something faintly metallic that lingered at the back of Zeek's tongue.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: It was only when he turned to speak—some half-formed instruction, the sort of thing he would once have tossed over his shoulder expecting BAH-lahg to answer before he had finished—that he realized how completely the silence had settled behind them.

lines.text: He turned back toward the doorway. The polished floor behind them lay undisturbed except for two sets of footprints leading into the library. Two. Not four.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He searched the room anyway, walking back to where the doorway had vanished, expecting to find a dropped pack, a broken weapon, some mark that proved memory had failed before reality had.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Only as he turned away did the weight pulling at his shoulder begin to feel unfamiliar. He shrugged off his pack and opened it. Tucked carefully beneath his bedroll lay BAH-lahg's spare axe head, wrapped in the same strip of cloth the big man always kept oiled to keep rust away. Zeek stared at it, certain it had not been there before.

lines.speaker: Narrator

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: They stood there, listening for the break in the silence, the sound of heavy footsteps or en-HEH-doo's dry voice reminding them that they were fools.

lines.text: The shelves grew stranger the deeper they walked.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: At first Zeek tried to make sense of them, searching for some order in the endless rows of glass. The labels suggested one existed. Every jar bore the same careful hand, each line etched into the base with deliberate precision. Subject. Variant. Outcome. Occasionally a number. Occasionally a single word. Whatever system governed the collection had never been intended for visitors. It assumed the reader already understood the rules.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: One contained nothing but a chair beneath a narrow window. Dust drifted lazily through a shaft of afternoon light that never changed, though no breeze stirred it. Another held a child carefully stacking smooth black stones into a tower that collapsed each time the last piece was set in place. The child never showed frustration. He simply began again, every movement identical to the last. Farther along, a woman sat before a table covered in maps, crossing out one route after another until the parchment itself disappeared beneath the ink.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: None of the figures acknowledged the world beyond the glass.

lines.text: He joined her. Inside the nearest jar a man stood in the middle of a desert, one hand raised to shield his eyes. Zeek watched him for several seconds before noticing that the figure's fingers had shifted almost imperceptibly. It was movement so gradual he might have mistaken it for imagination had he not been staring directly at it.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek had always imagined failure as something clean. A wrong decision. A closed door. A body buried beneath enough years that the living eventually stopped looking over their shoulders.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The City had found another use for it.

lines.text: Every abandoned path remained here, catalogued with the same care another civilization might have reserved for kings or sacred texts.

Exactly as he had taught Zeek when he was young enough to think the desert itself enjoyed swallowing careless men.

lines.text: They remained there another moment before moving on, neither willing to say aloud what both had begun to suspect.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: If Subject 001 still existed somewhere within the City, then perhaps nothing it collected was ever entirely gone.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The shelves continued for what felt like another hour, though neither of them trusted the passage of time anymore. The jars became less numerous as they walked. Empty spaces appeared between them at first, then entire shelves stood bare, their polished surfaces carrying only the faint outlines where glass had once rested. The rhythmic glow that had followed them through the library grew weaker until only a handful of vessels still answered one another across the darkness.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The last row ended without ceremony.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Beyond it stretched an open chamber, almost austere after the impossible abundance of the library behind them. There were no shelves here, no jars, no endless catalog of forgotten lives. At its center stood a single desk raised upon a pedestal fashioned from pale bone fused into black stone. Whatever had once belonged to either material had long since disappeared. They had become something new, seamless enough that Zeek could no longer tell where one ended and the other began.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Unlike the shelves behind them, the desk bore no dust.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Not recently. Not often. But regularly enough that the gray powder coating the rest of the library had never been allowed to settle there.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Zeek wasn't sure why he believed that, only that the certainty arrived before the thought itself. The library behind them no longer felt like a collection.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: It felt like the result of whatever happened here.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Resting upon the desk lay an enormous ledger opened to its middle pages. Beside it rested a single sharpened quill carved from the same calcified material as the key fused to Zeek's hand. They were not identical in shape, yet they belonged to one another as surely as a lock belonged to its key. The same gray veins ran through them. The same unnatural cold seemed to draw warmth from the air around them.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Neither of them reached for either object.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Instead Zeek stepped to the side of the desk and looked down at the open page.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The loops of the letters, the slight rightward slant, the habit of crossing a stroke twice whenever he wrote too quickly. He had spent enough nights copying inventories and caravan accounts to know his own hand better than his own face.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He had never written any of it.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The final entry described their arrival in the library. It described the empty shelves waiting beyond the jars. It described the disappearance of BAH-lahg and en-HEH-doo, the discovery of Subject 001, and words that still echoed in the chamber around them.

lines.speaker: Narrator

lines.text: Ninsun didn't answer immediately. She was studying the edge of the writing, watching where the ink thinned into the parchment.

lines.speaker: Ninsun
lines.text: Prophecy is written before it happens.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The blank pages that followed seemed far more unsettling than the words already written. They stretched on for hundreds of leaves, untouched except for the faint impressions left by the quill resting beside them, as though they had been prepared in advance and had simply been waiting for the story to arrive.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: It was carved from the same calcified stone that had become part of his hand. The same gray veins ran through it. The same impossible cold seemed to gather around it.

lines.speaker: Zik
lines.text: I don't think it wants one.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Ninsun never took her eyes off the open page.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Unlike the rest of the entry, it stood alone:
